The incubation biology of the New Zealand pigeon (Hemiphaga novaeseelandiae) reveals a tightly constrained developmental period. Field observations indicate that eggs, maintained at an internal nest temperature of 37.85 °C [T = 37.85 °C], typically hatch after approximately 28.5 days [ab = approximately 28.5 days], a duration consistent with that of other large columbids in temperate regions. The newly hatched chick, entirely dependent on crop milk, emerges at a wet weight of 18.6 grams [Wwb = 18.6 grams], a value extrapolated from measurements of the smallest neonates in the brood. This relatively modest mass at hatching underscores the altricial state of the nestling, which undergoes rapid somatic growth within the first weeks post-hatch. The precise thermal conditions of the nest cup, which are actively regulated by the incubating adult, appear critical for maintaining this developmental schedule, as deviations can prolong or shorten the incubation interval.

After hatching, the nestling enters a period of sustained parental provisioning and feather development. Under the thermal conditions typical of the active metabolic phase in this species (40.63 °C [T = 40.63 °C]), the pin-feathered chick achieves the capacity for sustained flight and leaves the nest at approximately 37 days after hatching [tx = approximately 37 days after hatching]. This fledging age, which falls squarely within the published range of 30 to 45 days, marks a significant milestone after which the juvenile begins to forage independently, though it may still receive occasional feeding from the attending adults. The transition from a brooded nestling to a fledgling is energetically demanding, and the timing of this event is closely tied to the availability of high-energy fruits in the local environment. Field records from several North Island populations corroborate this value, showing remarkably little inter-annual variation when food resources are stable.

Sexual maturation in Hemiphaga novaeseelandiae proceeds on a slower schedule compared to many smaller pigeon species. Following the fledgling independence stage, the growing juvenile undergoes a period of somatic consolidation and gonadal development. Under the same thermal regime of 40.63 °C [T = 40.63 °C], which reflects the core body temperature of active birds, puberty is attained at approximately 111 days after hatching [tp = approximately 111 days after hatching]. This timing likely reflects the need to reach a critical body size and condition before initiating the hormonal cascades that drive gametogenesis. The attainment of sexual maturity does not, however, immediately translate into breeding activity; first-year birds may be physiologically capable but are often excluded from nesting territories by older, more experienced conspecifics. The age at which the gonads become fully functional is therefore a conservative estimate of the species' minimal generation time.

The onset of the first reproductive effort is further deferred as the bird must secure a territory and a mate. Available data indicate that the time since birth at first brood is 365 days [tR = 365 days], meaning that most individuals do not breed until their second calendar year, again at the core body temperature of 40.63 °C [T = 40.63 °C]. This extended interval between puberty and first breeding is common among large, long-lived columbids and is considered a life-history strategy that prioritizes adult survival over early reproduction. Once established, breeding pairs are monogamous and exhibit a remarkably low reproductive output. Females lay a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch] and produce just one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year], which represents the maximum reproductive rate recorded for this species. This extremely low fecundity makes the population highly sensitive to increases in adult or nest mortality.

Longevity records for the New Zealand pigeon, derived from banding studies and comparative data from similar-sized columbids catalogued in the AnAge database, indicate that the maximum lifespan reaches approximately 20 years [am = approximately 20 years], assuming the active metabolic temperature of 40.63 °C [T = 40.63 °C] that defines its physiological baseline. This longevity, coupled with the very low annual reproductive rate of a single egg per clutch and a solitary annual clutch, frames a classic 'slow' life-history syndrome typical of island-endemic birds. Adult body mass ultimately stabilizes around 590 grams [Wwi = around 590 grams] in healthy, free-ranging individuals, though the documented range extends from 550 to 850 grams depending on sex, season, and local food abundance. This substantial size contributes to the pigeon's role as a key seed disperser for many native forest trees, and the species' demographic vulnerability is heightened by its delayed maturation and infrequent breeding events, making conservation intervention critical where predation pressure from introduced mammals is high.
